question: A three-class classifier outputs probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2, and the true class is the one given 0.3. Using the Brier score as defined in the lectures (mean over classes), what is the score?
option_a: 0.26, the squared gaps 0.25, 0.49 and 0.04 averaged over the three classes
option_b: 0.78, the squared gaps summed without averaging over the classes
option_c: 0.49, the squared gap of the true class alone
option_d: 0.70, one minus the probability given to the true class

question: Two classifiers each assign probability 0.9 to the correct class of a test instance. For the first, that class had prior probability 0.3; for the second, 0.8. Which gains more information score, and why?
option_a: The second, since a prediction that agrees with a high prior is more reliable
option_b: Both the same, since the score depends only on the posterior 0.9
option_c: Neither, since the score is zero whenever the predicted class is correct
option_d: The first, since the score is the log increase from prior to posterior and 0.3 to 0.9 is the larger jump

question: A screening test must miss as few sick patients as possible, while extra follow-up checks on healthy people are acceptable. Which F-beta setting matches this priority?
option_a: β = 0.5, since precision then dominates the score
option_b: β = 1, since F1 already weights recall above precision
option_c: β = 2, since recall then counts twice as important as precision
option_d: β = 0, since the score then reduces to recall alone

question: A classifier predicts the positive class only when its estimated probability exceeds a threshold. The threshold is raised from 0.5 to 0.9. What typically happens to precision and recall?
option_a: Recall tends to rise and precision tends to fall, since fewer negatives are predicted
option_b: Precision tends to rise and recall tends to fall, since only confident positives remain
option_c: Both rise, since a stricter rule makes fewer mistakes of either kind
option_d: Neither changes, since the trained model and its probabilities are unchanged

question: On a ROC curve, each point corresponds to one classification threshold. Where does the operating point move when the threshold is lowered, and why?
option_a: Down and to the left, since fewer items are called positive at a lower threshold
option_b: Along the diagonal, since lowering the threshold adds equal numbers of each error
option_c: Up and to the right, since more items are called positive, raising both true and false positives
option_d: Up and to the left, since true positives rise while false positives fall

question: A test set holds 100 positive and 900 negative samples. A classifier predicts 150 samples as positive, 80 of which are truly positive. What are its precision and recall?
option_a: Precision 0.80 and recall 0.53
option_b: Precision 0.91 and recall 0.80
option_c: Precision 0.53 and recall 0.80
option_d: Precision 0.53 and recall 0.91

question: A classifier produces 40 true positives, 10 false positives, 60 false negatives and 890 true negatives. What is its F1 score?
option_a: 0.60, the arithmetic mean of precision 0.80 and recall 0.40
option_b: 0.93, the fraction of all samples that were classified correctly
option_c: 0.80, since F1 takes the value of precision when recall is lower
option_d: 0.53, the harmonic mean of precision 0.80 and recall 0.40

question: The lectures recommend that class sizes be equal during training (avoiding domination). Which problem does this rule prevent?
option_a: Features of the majority class end up on a larger numeric scale than the rest
option_b: The training and testing sets become correlated through the shared majority class
option_c: The model leans toward the majority class, scoring high accuracy while recall on rare classes collapses
option_d: Cross-validation folds become too small to estimate the error reliably

question: In the 0.632 bootstrap, n instances are drawn with replacement for training and the undrawn instances are used for testing. Why does roughly 37% of the data end up in the test set?
option_a: The 63/37 split is fixed by hand as a compromise between bias and variance
option_b: Instances drawn more than once are moved to the test set, and about 37% are duplicates
option_c: Each instance is missed by all n draws with probability about 1/e, so about 36.8% are never drawn
option_d: Exactly a third of the data is reserved by the method before any sampling starts

question: Why do the lectures prefer k-fold cross-validation over repeatedly drawing random training and testing splits from the same data?
option_a: Random splits reuse the same instances across several test sets, so the runs are correlated
option_b: k-fold needs fewer model trainings, since one fold serves every repetition
option_c: Random splits cannot keep the class proportions equal in every run
option_d: k-fold uses each instance for training exactly once, which avoids overfitting

question: Activity data were recorded from ten people over several sessions each. The goal is to estimate how the classifier will perform on a person it has never seen. Which validation scheme fits best?
option_a: Leave-one-out over single instances, giving the largest possible training sets
option_b: The 0.632 bootstrap, since it reuses instances with replacement
option_c: Ten-fold cross-validation after randomly shuffling all instances
option_d: Leave-one-person-out, holding out all sessions of one subject per fold

question: A team selects features, tunes hyperparameters and reports the final score on the same single data set. What do the lectures say about such a result?
option_a: It is acceptable if the model is regularized strongly enough
option_b: It is acceptable as long as the data set is large enough
option_c: It is pessimistic, since no data was left aside for training
option_d: It is biased, since the reported score was influenced by choices made on the same data

question: In the semi-supervised scheme of the lectures, a classifier trained on few labelled samples labels the unlabelled ones and is retrained on both. Why weight the samples in the retraining?
option_a: To balance the class sizes between labelled and unlabelled data
option_b: To make the retraining converge in fewer iterations
option_c: To limit the influence of automatically assigned labels, which may be wrong
option_d: To normalize the feature scales of the unlabelled samples

question: Co-training trains several classifiers to label unlabelled data. How are the feature sets of these classifiers arranged, and what passes between them?
option_a: Heavily overlapping subsets; the classifiers exchange their weight vectors after each round
option_b: Disjoint, independent feature subsets; each adds its most confident predictions to the shared labelled set
option_c: Random bootstrap samples; the classifiers vote on every unlabelled sample at once
option_d: The same features with different models; the one with lowest training loss labels everything

question: Two classifiers both reach 75% accuracy, one measured on 100 test samples and the other on 1000. How do their 80% confidence intervals for the true success rate compare?
option_a: They are identical, since both observed the same success rate of 75%
option_b: The 100-sample interval is narrower, since fewer samples contain less noise
option_c: Only the 1000-sample result can be given a confidence interval at all
option_d: The 1000-sample interval is about three times narrower, since the estimate tightens with the test size

question: Features were standardized using the mean and standard deviation of the training set. How should the test set inputs be transformed?
option_a: With the test set's own mean and standard deviation, so it is also zero-mean
option_b: With the training set's mean and standard deviation, applied unchanged
option_c: Left untransformed, since the model has already been trained
option_d: With statistics recomputed on the pooled training and test data

question: In an insurance data set most claims are small and a few are very large. Why do the lectures warn against removing the large claims before modelling?
option_a: Removing them makes the variance too small for principal component analysis
option_b: They are genuine and carry most of the cost, so dropping them invalidates the model
option_c: Removing them violates the zero-mean assumption of the covariance matrix
option_d: The model would then overfit the many small claims that remain

question: The Relief algorithm scores a feature using, for each sample, the nearest distance to the same class and to the other classes. When is a feature rated most relevant?
option_a: When both nearest distances are small, showing the feature is stable
option_b: When it separates samples strongly from other classes and weakly from their own class
option_c: When both nearest distances are large, showing the feature spreads the data
option_d: When its Pearson correlation with the other features is highest

question: Consider the unit sphere in D dimensions and the thin shell between radius 1 and 1 - ε. What fraction of the volume lies in this shell, and what happens as D grows?
option_a: ε^D, which tends to 0, so the shell becomes negligible
option_b: ε, independent of D, so the shell always holds a fixed share
option_c: 1 - (1 - ε)^D, which tends to 1, so almost all volume sits near the surface
option_d: (1 - ε)^D, which tends to 1, so the interior holds almost all volume

question: With a fixed number of training samples, adding features first improves a classifier and then degrades it. What causes the decline?
option_a: The gradients shrink as more inputs are added, so training stalls
option_b: The samples become too sparse in the larger space to estimate the class distributions
option_c: Added features raise the learning rate beyond its stable range
option_d: The kernel trick stops working once the feature count exceeds the sample count

question: A multilayer perceptron with as many outputs as inputs and a single, smaller hidden layer with linear activations is trained to reproduce its input. What does the hidden layer compute at the optimum?
option_a: A projection onto the subspace of the leading principal components, the same as PCA
option_b: A nonlinear embedding that retains more variance than PCA
option_c: A random projection that preserves pairwise distances
option_d: The posterior probabilities of the classes in the data

question: After PCA with k components, the average squared projection error divided by the total variation equals 0.03. How much variance is retained, and does this meet the usual target?
option_a: 3% is retained, far below the usual target
option_b: 30% is retained, below the usual target
option_c: 97% is retained, but above the usual maximum of 90%
option_d: 97% is retained, within the usual target of 95 to 99%

question: Why do the lectures call the polynomial kernel (x1^T x2 + c)^D numerically unstable for large degree D?
option_a: The base raised to D collapses to 0 when it is below 1 and explodes when it is above 1
option_b: It requires the eigenvalues of the full Gram matrix at every evaluation
option_c: It is undefined whenever the inner product of the two vectors is negative
option_d: Its value depends on the absolute position of the data, so shifting it changes everything

question: For which kind of data do the lectures recommend a polynomial kernel over the RBF kernel?
option_a: Data that must be shifted without changing pairwise similarities
option_b: Data where the direction of the vectors matters more than their distance, such as bag-of-words documents
option_c: Data with a single class, where anomalies have to be enclosed
option_d: Data that is already linearly separable in the input space

question: A data set contains only recordings of a machine in normal operation. Which method from the lectures flags later anomalies, and which kernel is typically used?
option_a: A two-class SVM with a linear kernel trained on the normal data alone
option_b: A one-class SVM with an RBF kernel that encloses the region of normal samples
option_c: PCA keeping enough components to retain 99% of the variance
option_d: Co-training with the normal data as the labelled set

question: An SVM uses Gaussian kernels on two landmarks with weights w0 = -0.5, w1 = 1 and w2 = 1. A query point lies far from both landmarks. What does the hypothesis predict, and why?
option_a: Class 1, since the weights sum to 1.5, which is positive
option_b: Class 0, since both kernel values are near 0 and only the negative bias remains
option_c: Class 1, since the kernel value of a distant point approaches 1
option_d: No prediction, since points outside the landmarks are undefined

question: Why is latent semantic indexing applied to term-document matrices, and what does the truncated singular value decomposition provide?
option_a: The matrices are huge but sparse; the first k components give the closest k-dimensional representation
option_b: The term counts need standardization; the decomposition rescales each term to unit variance
option_c: The documents need clustering; the decomposition assigns each to one of k groups
option_d: The vocabulary contains stop words; the decomposition removes them automatically

question: A histogram density estimate is built from N = 200 samples with bins of width 0.5. One bin contains 30 samples. What is the estimated density in that bin?
option_a: 0.30, the count divided by N and by the bin width
option_b: 0.15, the count divided by N alone
option_c: 0.075, the count divided by N and multiplied by the bin width
option_d: 60, the count divided by the bin width alone

question: Why do the lectures describe histogram methods as well suited to very large data sets?
option_a: The bins adapt their width automatically to the local sample density
option_b: The estimate needs no choice of bin width, so it has no parameters
option_c: The method keeps working in high dimensions without extra samples
option_d: Once the bin counts are collected, the individual data items can be discarded

question: A Parzen estimator uses one kernel width for the whole space. What goes wrong in regions of high and of low sample density?
option_a: High-density regions become noisy while low-density regions are over-smoothed
option_b: High-density regions are over-smoothed while low-density regions give noisy estimates
option_c: Both kinds of region are over-smoothed by the same amount
option_d: The estimate integrates to more than one in high-density regions

question: Both the Parzen estimator and the k-nearest-neighbour density estimate use the form p(x) = K / (N V). What is the difference between the two?
option_a: Parzen fixes K and grows V; the neighbour method fixes V and counts K
option_b: Both fix V, but the neighbour method replaces the hypercube with a Gaussian kernel
option_c: Parzen fixes V and counts K; the neighbour method fixes K and grows V until K points fit
option_d: The neighbour method estimates N from the data instead of using the sample size

question: The Parzen estimator can count points with a hard-edged hypercube window. Why do the lectures replace it with a Gaussian kernel?
option_a: The hard window boundaries produce artificial discontinuities in the density estimate
option_b: The Gaussian kernel needs no normalization constant in D dimensions
option_c: The hypercube cannot be defined in more than three dimensions
option_d: The Gaussian makes the estimate independent of the sample size N

question: A k-nearest-neighbour classifier with K = 7 finds 4 neighbours of class A, 2 of class B and 1 of class C. What posterior does the derivation in the lectures assign to class A?
option_a: 4/7, since the class-conditional density and the class prior combine to the share of class A among the K
option_b: 4/N, since the posterior depends on the total training set size N
option_c: 1/3, one equal share for each class present among the neighbours
option_d: 4/7 only if the classes were equally frequent in the training set

question: When building a kD-tree for nearest-neighbour search, how do the lectures choose the split axis and split point, and why?
option_a: A random axis at a random point, to avoid any bias toward one dimension
option_b: The axis of least variance, split at its mean, to keep regions narrow
option_c: The axis of greatest variance, split at its median, giving balanced and roughly square regions
option_d: Always the first axis, split at its mean, so the tree is simple to traverse

question: A query descends a kD-tree to the leaf region that contains it. Why must the search still examine the parent and sibling regions before returning the nearest neighbour?
option_a: Leaf regions never store points, only the internal nodes do
option_b: A nearer point may lie just across a splitting boundary in a neighbouring region
option_c: The tree has to be rebalanced after every query is answered
option_d: The class labels of the points are stored in the sibling regions

question: Why do kD-trees lose efficiency in high dimensions, and what does a ball tree change?
option_a: kD-trees cannot index more than three dimensions; ball trees index any number
option_b: kD-trees require the data to be sorted first; ball trees accept unsorted data
option_c: kD-trees are always unbalanced; ball trees are balanced by construction
option_d: Rectangle corners lie far from the centre, so many branches get checked; ball trees use hyperspheres

question: A decision tree root has entropy 0.997. The weighted child entropies of four candidate splits are WiFi 0.868, accelerometer 0.756, audio 0.884 and light 0.948. Which split is chosen, and why?
option_a: Accelerometer, since the lowest remaining entropy gives the largest information gain of 0.241
option_b: Light, since its children retain the most information at 0.948
option_c: WiFi, since it has the most branches and splits the data most finely
option_d: Audio, since 0.884 lies closest to the parent entropy

question: A tree node holds 8 samples of class yes and 2 of class no. What is its entropy in bits?
option_a: About 0.80
option_b: Exactly 1.00
option_c: About 0.32
option_d: About 0.72

question: A sensor feature is missing for some instances. Which two treatments do the lectures propose for decision trees?
option_a: Drop every instance with a missing value, or drop the feature entirely
option_b: Replace the value with the feature mean, or replace it with zero
option_c: Retrain the tree without the feature, or stop splitting at that node
option_d: Add a binary is-missing feature, or send the instance down every branch weighted by training frequencies

question: In the pruning example of the lectures, the leaves below a node have a combined pessimistic error estimate of 0.51, while replacing the node by a single leaf gives 0.46. What is done, and why?
option_a: The children are kept, since more structure always lowers the training error
option_b: The node is split further to bring the estimate below 0.46
option_c: The children are pruned, since the single leaf's estimated error is lower than the subtree's
option_d: The tree is rebuilt with a larger confidence value until both estimates match

question: When deciding whether to prune, the lectures use an upper confidence limit on the error rate rather than the observed error at each leaf. Why?
option_a: The observed error on training data is always zero at the leaves
option_b: It guarantees that the pruned tree has zero error on the test set
option_c: It makes computing the entropy of the leaves unnecessary
option_d: Observed error on a few samples is unreliable, and the upper limit penalizes small leaves more

question: Random forests draw a random subset of features at every candidate split in addition to bagging. Why is this extra randomization needed?
option_a: Strong features would otherwise dominate every tree, making the trees dependent and weakening the averaging
option_b: It lowers the bias of each individual tree by letting it see fewer features
option_c: It speeds up prediction, since fewer features need to be read at test time
option_d: It removes the need to draw bootstrap samples, since the splits are already random

question: In backpropagation as presented, the error of an output unit is its activation minus the target. How is the error of a hidden unit obtained?
option_a: Passing the next layer's errors back through the transposed weights, times the activation derivative
option_b: Subtracting the mean target from the hidden unit's activation
option_c: Taking the gradient of the regularization term alone for that unit
option_d: Copying the output error back unchanged to every hidden unit

question: Why must the weights of a neural network be initialized randomly rather than all set to the same value?
option_a: Equal weights give every unit of a layer the same error signal, so they stay identical copies
option_b: Equal weights make the loss function undefined at the first step
option_c: Random weights guarantee convergence to the global minimum
option_d: Equal weights make the forward pass overflow numerically

question: A network has two output units. The first has activation 0.9 with target 1; the second has activation 0.2 with target 0. What are their backpropagation errors delta?
In the backpropagation formula the propagated error is multiplied element-wise by the derivative of the activation function. What does this factor do?
option_a: It normalizes the error vector of the layer to unit length
option_b: It scales the error by the activation's local slope, so a saturated unit passes almost no error back
option_c: It selects which units are pruned from the network
option_d: It adds the gradient of the regularization term to the error

question: A fully connected layer maps 1000 inputs to 1000 outputs. A one-dimensional convolutional layer with a filter of width 3 produces the same 1000 outputs. Ignoring biases, roughly how many weights does each need?
option_a: About one million for the fully connected layer and three for the convolutional layer
option_b: About one million for both, since both produce 1000 outputs
option_c: About a thousand for the fully connected layer and three for the convolutional layer
option_d: Three for both, since both compute weighted sums of neighbours

question: A filter with values -1 and 1 on two adjacent pixels and 0 elsewhere is slid across an image row. What does its output show?
option_a: The local average of neighbouring pixels, which blurs the image
option_b: The largest pixel value in each window, as in max pooling
option_c: Values near zero on uniform regions and large magnitude where neighbouring pixels differ, i.e. edges
option_d: Positive values proportional to the local brightness of the image

question: Which limitation of ordinary feed-forward and convolutional networks do the lectures give as the motivation for recurrent networks?
option_a: They cannot use non-linear activation functions, so they only model linear maps
option_b: They cannot be trained with backpropagation once they have more than one hidden layer
option_c: They need labelled data, while recurrent networks can learn from unlabelled sequences
option_d: They require a fixed-size input and a fixed number of layers, so sequences of varying length do not fit

question: An unrolled recurrent network is drawn as many copies of the same network, each passing information to the next. What does 'the same' mean for the parameters, and what follows from it?
option_a: Each time step has its own weights, so the sequence length must be fixed in advance
option_b: The weights are copied once and then trained separately for every step
option_c: The copies share only the bias terms and learn separate weight matrices
option_d: One set of weights is applied at every time step, so sequences of any length can be processed

question: A plain recurrent network completes 'The sun rises in the' with 'morning' but fails to complete 'I practice Finnish since 5 years ... I am fluent in' correctly. Why?
option_a: The second sentence has more words than the hidden state can store
option_b: Recurrent networks cannot represent proper nouns such as language names
option_c: The first sentence appeared in the training data and the second did not
option_d: The needed clue is many steps back, and its influence on the weights fades as the temporal gap grows

question: How does an LSTM cell differ structurally from the plain recurrent cell presented in the lectures, and what is the purpose of the difference?
option_a: It replaces the tanh layer with a convolutional layer to reduce the parameter count
option_b: Four interacting neural network layers instead of one tanh layer, built to keep information for long periods
option_c: It removes the recurrent connection so that gradients cannot vanish
option_d: It stacks two plain recurrent cells to double the size of the state

question: For which kind of input would a three-dimensional convolution be appropriate according to the lectures?
option_a: Inputs on a 3D grid, such as video frames over time or volumetric medical scans
option_b: Colour images, with one dimension for each of the three colour channels
option_c: Text, using a context window of three words at a time
option_d: Grayscale images, with the third dimension indexing the filters

question: The lectures describe a feed-forward network as logistic regression whose features are learned in the first stage. Which consequence follows?
option_a: The network can only separate classes that are linearly separable in the input
option_b: The hidden layer must use a linear activation function
option_c: The hidden layer replaces hand-engineered features and the output layer is a logistic classifier on them
option_d: The network needs no gradient information for training

question: The regularized logistic loss adds λ over 2m times the sum of squared weights to the data term. What happens to the model as λ is made very large?
option_a: The loss on the training data goes to zero
option_b: The weights are driven toward zero, so the model becomes simpler and may underfit
option_c: The sigmoid becomes steeper, so predictions become more confident
option_d: The number of features used by the model increases

question: For a training sample with label y = 1, the logistic loss term is minus the log of the predicted probability h(x). What happens to this term as h(x) approaches 0?
option_a: It approaches 1, the maximum value of the loss
option_b: It approaches 0, so the sample stops contributing
option_c: It becomes negative and starts to reward the prediction
option_d: It grows without bound, so a confident wrong prediction is penalized heavily

question: The SVM objective in the lectures is C times the summed cost terms plus one half the sum of squared weights. What is the effect of choosing a very large C?
option_a: The weights are shrunk toward zero, which widens the margin
option_b: The width σ of the Gaussian kernel increases
option_c: Errors on training points dominate, so the margin narrows and overfitting becomes likelier
option_d: The landmarks are removed from the hypothesis

question: A linear-kernel SVM and logistic regression both learn a linear decision function. What is the main difference in how they are trained?
option_a: The loss: the SVM minimizes margin-based cost terms, logistic regression minimizes the log loss
option_b: The SVM cannot include a regularization term
option_c: Logistic regression needs a kernel function to be trained
option_d: The SVM outputs calibrated class probabilities, logistic regression does not

question: In the neural network loss of the lectures, a sample with C output units contributes which terms for a one-hot target?
option_a: Only the output of the true class, since the other targets are zero
option_b: All C outputs: minus log h for the true class and minus log (1 - h) for every other class
option_c: Only the largest output among the wrong classes, as a margin term
option_d: The mean of the C outputs, compared with the mean of the targets

question: The regularization strength λ trades data fit against small weights. According to the lectures' data-handling rules, how should its value be chosen?
option_a: By setting it to the number of training samples m
option_b: By fixing it from the slope of the sigmoid function
option_c: By hyperparameter tuning on a data set separate from both the training and the final test set
option_d: By choosing the value that minimizes the error on the test set
